sections.title: Objective type questions: each has two parts of 1 mark (fill in the blanks, true/false, match or one word).

questions.q: Fill in the blanks: (a) The resistance of a semiconductor ______ with increase in temperature. (b) The numbers of holes and free electrons are equal in an ______ semiconductor.
Fill in the blanks: (a) A ______ is a specially doped p-n junction that works in the breakdown region. (b) The width of the depletion layer ______ when the junction is reverse biased.
(a) When a p-n junction is forward biased, the depletion width ______. (b) A Zener diode is used as a ______.

sections.title: Very short answer questions. Answer in 30–50 words.

questions.q: Write two differences between intrinsic and extrinsic semiconductors.
questions.answer:
(1) Intrinsic is pure; extrinsic is doped with a trivalent or pentavalent impurity.
(2) In intrinsic nₑ = n_h and conductivity is low; in extrinsic one carrier is in the majority and conductivity is much higher.

questions.q: What is meant by the unidirectional (rectifying) property of a p-n junction? Give one application.
questions.answer: It conducts easily in forward bias but hardly at all in reverse bias, so current flows in one direction only. Application: a rectifier converting ac to dc.

questions.q: Name a diode used in reverse bias and state its use.
questions.answer: A Zener diode (in reverse breakdown), used as a voltage regulator. (A photodiode is also used in reverse bias, to detect light.)

or.q: Looking at a p-n junction diode, how do you identify its p and n ends? Why is it required?
or.answer: The end marked with a band (or the bar in the symbol) is the cathode, i.e. the n-side; the other is the p-side (anode). A diode conducts only when p is at the higher potential, so it must be connected the right way round in a circuit.

questions.q: How is the conductivity of a semiconductor affected by a rise in temperature? Explain.
questions.answer: It increases. More electrons gain enough energy to jump from the valence band to the conduction band, creating more free electrons and holes.

questions.q: Draw the symbols of n-p-n and p-n-p transistors.
questions.answer: Both have emitter, base and collector. n-p-n: the arrow on the emitter points outward (away from the base). p-n-p: the arrow points inward (towards the base). The arrow shows the conventional current in the emitter.

or.q: Draw energy band diagrams of a semiconductor and an insulator, showing the gap.
or.answer: Semiconductor: valence band and conduction band separated by a small gap (about 1 eV — Si 1.1 eV, Ge 0.7 eV). Insulator: a large gap (more than about 3–6 eV, e.g. diamond about 6 eV), so electrons cannot cross.

sections.title: Short answer questions. Answer in 50–80 words.

questions.q: Define forward bias and reverse bias. Plot the variation of current with applied voltage for a p-n junction.
questions.answer:
Forward bias: p-side to the positive and n-side to the negative terminal; the barrier is lowered and current flows easily.
Reverse bias: p-side to negative and n-side to positive; the barrier is raised and only a tiny current flows.
Graph: in forward bias the current is almost zero up to the knee voltage (Si about 0.7 V), then rises steeply. In reverse bias a small, nearly constant reverse current flows (µA) until breakdown, when it rises suddenly.

questions.q: Germanium doped with indium (X) and germanium doped with arsenic (Y) are joined and connected to a variable battery. (a) Name the types of X and Y. (b) Is the junction forward or reverse biased? (c) Sketch the V–I graph.
questions.answer:
(a) Indium is trivalent, so X is p-type; arsenic is pentavalent, so Y is n-type.
(b) If the positive terminal is connected to X (p) it is forward biased; if to Y (n), reverse biased.
(c) Forward: current rises sharply after about 0.3 V (Ge). Reverse: only a tiny current until breakdown.

questions.q: Explain how an intrinsic semiconductor is converted into (i) n-type and (ii) p-type, with examples and energy band diagrams.
questions.answer:
(i) n-type: dope Si/Ge with a pentavalent atom (P, As, Sb). Four electrons bond and the fifth is nearly free. A donor level just below the conduction band supplies electrons, which are the majority carriers.
(ii) p-type: dope with a trivalent atom (B, Al, Ga, In). One bond is incomplete, creating a hole. An acceptor level just above the valence band takes electrons, leaving holes as the majority carriers.

sections.title: Long answer questions. Answer in 80–120 words.

questions.q: Explain with circuit diagrams how a p-n junction diode works in (i) forward and (ii) reverse bias, and draw its V–I characteristics.
questions.answer:
Formation: diffusion of electrons and holes across the junction leaves a depletion layer with a barrier potential (Si about 0.7 V).
(i) Forward bias (p to +): the applied voltage opposes the barrier, the depletion layer narrows, majority carriers cross, and a large current flows after the knee voltage. Circuit: battery, diode, milliammeter, voltmeter and rheostat.
(ii) Reverse bias (p to −): the barrier rises and the depletion layer widens; only minority carriers give a tiny reverse current (µA), until breakdown. Circuit: battery reversed, with a microammeter.
Characteristic: a steep rise in the first quadrant after the knee; a small nearly flat current in the third quadrant, then a sudden rise at breakdown.

questions.q: Classify solids as conductors, semiconductors and insulators on the basis of energy bands. Give two differences between intrinsic and extrinsic semiconductors.
questions.answer:
Conductors: the valence and conduction bands overlap, so many free electrons conduct even at low temperature.
Semiconductors: a small gap (about 1 eV); at room temperature some electrons cross, giving moderate conductivity that rises with temperature.
Insulators: a wide gap (more than 3 eV); practically no electrons cross, so there is no conduction.
Intrinsic vs extrinsic: (1) pure vs doped; (2) nₑ = n_h vs a majority carrier (electrons in n-type, holes in p-type); conductivity is low vs high.

or.q: Explain the formation of a p-n junction. Draw a diagram and define the depletion region and barrier potential.
or.answer:
When p- and n-type materials are joined, holes diffuse from p to n and electrons from n to p, where they recombine. This leaves immobile negative acceptor ions on the p-side and positive donor ions on the n-side near the junction.
This thin region, empty of free carriers, is the depletion region. The ions set up an electric field and a potential difference, the barrier potential (about 0.7 V for Si, 0.3 V for Ge), which stops further diffusion.
